segments.text: Every thought, movement, emotion and sensation involves biological activity. This does not mean behaviour is caused only by biology; it means the brain, nerves and hormones provide the physical systems through which behaviour occurs.
The easiest way to study this unit is to move from the smallest level to the larger system: neuron → nervous system → brain/spinal cord → peripheral nerves → endocrine system → behaviour.

items.text: Neuron and its function

: A neuron is a specialized cell that receives, processes and transmits information. Dendrites generally receive signals, the cell body maintains the cell, and the axon carries signals toward terminals. Communication within a neuron is electrical; communication between many neurons occurs chemically across synapses through neurotransmitters.
Central nervous system

: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord. The brain coordinates complex functions such as perception, movement, memory and emotion, while the spinal cord carries information and supports reflex activity.
Peripheral nervous system

: The peripheral nervous system connects the central nervous system with the rest of the body. The somatic system is strongly related to voluntary movement and sensory information; the autonomic system regulates many automatic bodily processes. The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions usually prepare the body for action and help restore calmer functioning, respectively.
Endocrine system

: Endocrine glands release hormones into the bloodstream. Hormonal effects are generally slower than fast neural signalling but can last longer. Behaviour-related examples include stress responses, metabolism, growth and reproductive functions.
Biology and behaviour

: A strong answer links a biological structure with a behavioural function but avoids biological determinism. Behaviour usually emerges from interaction among biology, learning, environment and culture.

blocks.text: The neuron as the basic signalling unit

items.text: Dendrites and cell body

: Dendrites receive many incoming signals, while the cell body supports the neuron's metabolism and integrates information. The simplified textbook picture is useful, but real neurons vary greatly in shape and function.
Axon and action potential

: When excitation reaches threshold, an action potential travels along the axon. It is an all-or-none electrical event: stronger stimulation is represented mainly through firing patterns and rates rather than a 'bigger' individual action potential.
Myelin
: Myelin insulates many axons and allows faster saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier. Damage to myelin can therefore disrupt efficient neural communication.
Synapse and neurotransmission

: At many synapses an electrical signal triggers release of neurotransmitter molecules, which cross a small synaptic gap and bind to receptors on another cell. Effects may be excitatory, inhibitory or modulatory depending on receptor and circuit.
Neurotransmitters

: Dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA and other transmitters participate in many functions. Avoid the common mistake of assigning one transmitter to one emotion or disorder; effects depend on pathways, receptors and broader networks.
Central nervous system

: The brain and spinal cord form the CNS. The spinal cord carries sensory and motor information and supports reflexes; the brain integrates information across distributed networks rather than relying on one isolated 'centre' for every complex behaviour.
Peripheral nervous system

: The PNS connects the CNS with muscles, organs and sensory receptors. The somatic division is strongly involved in voluntary skeletal movement and sensory input, while the autonomic division regulates internal organs.
Sympathetic division
: This division supports mobilization during challenge by altering heart rate, blood flow and other bodily functions. It is adaptive when matched to demands; it is not a 'bad' system.
Parasympathetic division

: This division supports restoration, digestion and energy conservation. Healthy regulation depends on flexible coordination between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity rather than permanent dominance of one.

blocks.text: Major brain regions and behavioural functions

items.text: Brainstem
: Structures in and around the brainstem regulate essential functions such as breathing, arousal and basic reflexes. Damage can therefore have widespread effects.
Cerebellum
: The cerebellum is central to coordination, balance and motor learning and also participates in some cognitive processes. It illustrates why brain regions often have multiple interacting functions.
Limbic-related structures

: The amygdala contributes to processing biologically significant stimuli and learning about threat; the hippocampal formation is crucial for forming certain new declarative memories. Neither structure should be described as the single 'seat' of fear or memory.
Cerebral cortex

: The cortex contains specialized but interconnected regions. Frontal areas are important for planning, inhibition, working memory and voluntary action; parietal areas integrate somatosensory and spatial information; temporal regions support hearing, language and memory functions; occipital cortex is central to vision.
Hemispheric specialization

: Some functions show lateralization, such as strong left-hemisphere involvement in language for many people. Popular claims that people are simply 'left-brained' or 'right-brained' are misleading because normal cognition depends on extensive communication between hemispheres.

blocks.text: Endocrine system and slower chemical regulation

items.text: Hormones

: Endocrine glands release hormones into the bloodstream. Hormonal signalling is generally slower than neural signalling and can produce longer-lasting effects on metabolism, growth, reproduction and stress responses.
Hypothalamus-pituitary relationship
: The hypothalamus helps link neural and endocrine control. Through the pituitary and other endocrine pathways, it contributes to regulation of growth, reproduction, stress and homeostasis.
Stress example

: A sudden threat can involve rapid sympathetic activation together with endocrine processes such as the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The example shows that neural and hormonal systems work together rather than as separate competing explanations.

segments.text: Genes influence the development and functioning of nervous systems, but genes do not mechanically determine complex behaviour. Gene expression and behavioural outcomes depend on developmental and environmental conditions. Heritability describes variation within a population under particular conditions; it does not tell us that an individual trait is fixed.

Neuroplasticity refers to the nervous system's capacity to change with development, learning, injury and experience. Plasticity has limits, but it is a direct reason to avoid biological determinism: experience can modify neural connections, and biological conditions can alter how experience is processed.

Use stress as one integrating example to connect brain, autonomic nervous system and hormones.

rows: Avoid this error Do not say the sympathetic system is “bad” and the parasympathetic system is “good.” Both are necessary parts of normal regulation.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Use a labelled diagram first, then explain neuron function, CNS, PNS and endocrine system in sequence. Add a short real-life example such as a sudden threat to show how the systems work together.
• Neurons are basic information-processing cells of the nervous system.
• The CNS is brain plus spinal cord; the PNS links the CNS with the body.
• The autonomic nervous system regulates many involuntary functions.
• Hormones are chemical messengers carried through the bloodstream.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
